16. In the Chapter on the Conclusion, 18 verses:
He who is the eye of the world like the sun with its thousand rays; who is the abode of lights like the sun;
who has opened the door to liberation like the sun; and who, like the sun, brings an end to darkness.
The Self of all embodied beings is like the sun, like the moon, and is fashioned by Time;
may that Creator, who is incomparable to others, make our speech auspicious.
I shall speak concerning a king who is endowed with virtues, whose time of birth is known and whose fortune is distinguished;
or else one whose birth is unknown, or whose future fortune is not yet understood.
By means of the hundreds of extensive omens concerning sea voyages that have been fully described.
Karma produced in another birth—whether good or bad—is destiny (*daiva*);
that alone brings about [one's status] in a birth such as a noble family. Beyond childhood, there is also the state of being a worthy recipient of discipline and excellence.
This must be established as being like agriculture performed by men and gods; therefore, one should exert oneself.
O King, the attainment of results by a ruler is like that of a farmer, occurring through both fate and human effort;
yet if there is even a single flaw, everything goes to ruin, just as water flows out from a hole in a leather bag.
If the king himself were a knower of destiny, he would be the very cause of success for one desiring to go forth.
If he were the cause of success for one seeking victory over enemies,
why then would the king not be his domestic priest?

Even ministers who have mastered the treatises on spiritual awakening and worldly affairs should not offer obeisance to sovereigns, even if those kings possess noble birth, elephants, horses, and infantry.
There would be no dependence on a sheath or the like for that which is primary.
One who is content in his own land when he possesses elephants,

horses, and a treasury, and does not march forth with his armies, will meet with humiliation from others and go to ruin; or else, he will have his wealth and kingdom destroyed by his own people alone.
He who has gone [to the goal], who does not seize others—being one whose conduct follows the excellent path—he is far removed from the ways of worldly policy.
The owl is subdued by the crow at night, and that same crow is under the power of the crows during the day;
the lion kills the crocodile on land, while the aquatic creature kills the lion in the water. Likewise, a king who passes his time without awareness [of the proper occasion] perishes.
When one is overcome by hatred and pride, he remembers the words of the wise while under the power of his enemies.
Having shown contempt for the enemy and believing "I have conquered" due to the power of intoxication,
one must not abandon effort; for even a slight enemy is like a venomous serpent.
A lordly elephant, intoxicated and struck down by men with forces numbering ten thousand from a mountain thicket,
lies bound to a pillar, scraping away the decorative streaks of ichor.
Having made his fortress secure for his own protection, provided with elephants, horses, physicians, artisans, and Brahmins;

having cleared it of greedy, terrified, arrogant, or enraged wicked officials, and ensuring it is inhabited by brave and trustworthy men— the lord of men, with his rear-flanks pure, may advance against the territory of the enemy.

Having understood the strength of both his own and the enemy's forces, he should employ conciliation through various gifts, as well as strategic means for protecting against calamities and the approaches of battle;
he should win over the virtuous with devotion and those greedy for wealth with gifts.
One should not win over those who cannot be won even by the three means of policy; rather, one should subdue them with punishments.
The Moon is the lord of Sama; Mercury, along with Mars and the Sun, are the lords of Danda; the Moon is the lord of Dana; and Jupiter, Saturn, and Mercury, together with Rahu, are the lords of Bheda.
[These results arise] when they are endowed with strength, situated in Upachaya houses, or placed in the Ascendant or other strong positions (Kendras).
That very thing attains accomplishment on those days, or even through their respective degrees (aṃśaka).
Among the six measures of statecraft, peace (*sandhi*) comes first, followed by war (*vigraha*) involving a negotiated treaty;
if these two are not possible, then there is staying put (*āsana*), marching with the entire army (*yāna*) to invade the enemy’s city,
or marching with half the army (*dvaidhībhāva-yāna*) when attacked, which is said to be the march toward the enemy's city while divided.
That which is a conjunction elsewhere is indeed declared to be another [type of] connection (saṃśraya) of qualities.
At midday, the sun is known as Ākranda;
at dawn, it is Paura; and when situated at the end [of the day], it is Yāyin.
Jupiter, Saturn, and the son of the Moon (Mercury) are likewise Paura.
The Ketu planet, as well as Saturn, Mars, Siddhi, and Kānandana, are all wanderers.

When the citizens who perform auspicious deeds are endowed with vigor, they provide vehicles for those traveling and seats for those seeking rest; when the citizens performing auspicious deeds, along with the travelers and the planets, fall into a state of duality, there is peace through the gentle planets and victory in battle through powerful and favorable malefic planets.
Even if all [the planets] are bestowers of inauspiciousness, the king should take refuge in the one favored by fate.

For the treasury is indeed the root of the tree of sovereignty; therefore, what can a rival do to destroy it, just as a bird cannot destroy its own wings? Just as the collection of sense-faculties depends on food, so too does food depend upon wealth.
One should be diligent in attaining that [virtue], in preserving it, and in increasing it.
The kingdom must be protected by the king; therefore, he should maintain its treasury.
He should collect taxes from those who are appropriate at the proper time, and he should not demand wealth such that it would cause public censure.

A king’s expedition in autumn or in spring yields the desired fruit; some say there is no restriction regarding an enemy’s vulnerability. Yet, even when the enemy is vulnerable, success occurs only for one who is favored by fate.
This common material gift belongs equally to all the lords of the earth.
The king should command a minister who is endowed with auspicious destiny to slay an enemy who is himself devoid of destiny;
yet even one devoted to destiny should not abandon his purpose.
When the island has been seen, what is the purpose of following the tracks of the elephant?
Time approaches a man but once, somehow;
he who awaits that time does not attain it.
Time disregards the prey that has come within its range.
Even a python, though slow in its movement, attains success.
A fruit situated in a difficult place, though unripe, does not bring about success for men even with great effort; nor does it produce any benefit,
since it would be common property and liable to fall.
At the proper time, that which is joined with the fallen [planets] becomes flavorful for one's happiness.
For just as the colors red, black, and so forth belong to the sky, yet appear correctly white upon it,
even so do the qualities of the *lagna*, lunar day (*tithi*), and other factors belong to a traveler who is free from defects.
Wine, women, instrumental music, dance, song, dice, idle wandering, hunting, excessive sleep, and backbiting—
one should know these to be the ten vices born of desire that afflict men.

Harshness of speech, harshness of punishment, envy, malice, jealousy, slander, violence, and the disparagement of wealth—this group of eight is declared to arise from anger. They say that this liquor is a great seat of misconduct; it is a small wealth that serves to ravage the mind, the intellect, and the excellence of one's being.

With his intellect impaired by that [intoxication], because his primary faculty is focused on it, he does not indeed distinguish between what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit, nor other such things.
Under the sway of intoxication, one regards even one's mother as a wife, and a wife as a mother;
one regards even a crumbling stone house as a pit, and a well as a home;
through delusion, one regards a mere trifle of water as the ocean, and the lord of waters as dry land.
He even treats the king as a friend; what else would a drinker of intoxicants not do?
Furthermore, having lost, he plays again out of a mere desire for victory; sometimes he even obtains that which is more distinguished.
Having done unpleasant things through intoxication, and having tormented others on all sides, the king drinks yet more, seeking further distinctions of vice.

One may, at will, drink [wine] that does not impair the intellect, following the festive instructions of physicians; yet, apart from gambling, there are no sensual pleasures that are truly beneficial when practiced with discernment. For what is the fruit of life for a wise man if it is devoid of the objects of the senses?
Devoid of purity and proper conduct, like a corpse abandoned by friends and kinsmen,
he is fearless, shameless, and pitiless, obtaining food only with great difficulty;
for him there is no kinsman, no bond, and no oath, nor does he regard the two worlds.
He is a deceiver, a defiler of his family, a gambler, a mine of faults [or an ocean of faults], and devoid of happiness.
That king who, his own mind corrupted by his own wicked conduct, does not heed the words of astrologers, ministers, friends, and trusted advisors— he,
deprived of a capable leader, like a blind man, soon falls into the territory of his enemies and becomes an object of ridicule.
Intelligent, wise, of unimpaired speech, skillful, patient, upright,

righteous, free from envy, prompt in action, a knower of the sixfold policy, powerful, energetic, a perceiver of the enemy's weaknesses, steadfast, and one who knows the conditions of growth, decline, and stability.
He who is brave, does not forget a favor received, and serves the elderly is not one who falls into calamity.
One should act after careful examination and not be boastful; one should be firm in one's resolve and exceedingly steadfast in what one has undertaken.
One should have the senses conquered, and likewise have conquered anger, greed, sleep, sloth, and attachment to one's dwelling place.
One who is generous, humble, pleasant to behold, free from delusion, and endowed with practical application;
one who understands the divisions of place and time, and who personally observes the conduct of affairs.
One who is skilled in the logic of words and their meanings, yet not overly clever; one who is bold, proficient in the arts of war, and of noble birth;
one who speaks with a smile, speaking measuredly and truthfully—one who is endowed with such [qualities], or he who possesses them, is the abode of prosperity.
Even if it is endowed with all virtues, an expedition given to an unworthy person is like a maiden given to one lacking merit;
it brings disgrace and the loss of happiness and wealth to the donor who is dull-witted regarding the knowledge of other suitable recipients.
However, an expedition performed through the conjunction of auspicious asterisms, planets, and the ascendant produces merit for one who is indeed possessed of virtue.
For one who is possessed of faults, [the teaching] is useless even if endowed with virtues, like a lute devoid of its sounding board.
Even a perfectly pure conduct, when practiced with equanimity, yields fruits according to the capacity of the recipient.
For even the intense radiance of Indra does not dispel the darkness upon the earth.
At the end of the night, one should reflect upon the affairs of those residing within the circles of enemies and friends,
as well as the tasks completed and uncompleted by those appointed to positions of power, wealth, and territory, and by those who have sought refuge.
Whether it be one who is independent, renowned for his virtues, a supreme hero, or a virtuous person praised by all—
having reflected that such a person has come to my country and should be honored for the sake of winning over the people, [I shall do so].
Having previously been awakened from sleep by the sound of flutes, lutes, and small drums, along with song,
he should leave his bed at the conclusion of the musical instruments, while listening to the auspicious words of the reciters.
One should not eat tooth-sticks that have not been used before, nor those provided with leaves;
nor those that are dried at the top, nor those that are split, nor those with even joints, nor those without bark.
Facing either north or east, standing straight and with the [teeth-stick] free of cracks and measuring one span (vitasti) in length,
the king, having restrained his speech and rinsed [his mouth], should eat it and then discard it in a clean place.
Falling directly toward [the observer], situated in a peaceful direction, and standing upright—these are auspicious and exceedingly beautiful.
Conversely, it is declared that falling otherwise produces inauspicious results; however, when it falls while remaining stationary, it makes food delicious.
Having first prostrated before the gods and his own gurus, and having given a cow with its calf to a brahmin,
he should look at his face in clarified butter and in a mirror, and then hear [the announcement of] the lunar mansion and the lunar day.
Having heard the lunar day, the asterism, the planets, and the day, one obtains virtue, wealth, fame, and happiness;
as well as health, long life, victory, sons, the destruction of bad dreams, and popularity in the world.
Having partaken of white garments, turbans, fine gold, and jewels, one should follow the words of physicians.
With smiles, graciousness, and being the first to speak, with a look of favor and the taking of hands in greeting—
thus appeasing even the hearts of his enemies according to their fitness— he should resort to the assembly hall of Dharma.

Wearing modest dress and ornaments, raising his right hand, endowed with discernment, and seated comfortably or even standing, the king— regardless of whether he has enemies or friends— should preside over the administration of justice.
One should not think, "I am endowed with patience," and thus practice forgiveness toward those deserving of punishment; for that is no true dharma.
Indeed, the power of punishment belongs to the wicked, in whose hands the multitude of the virtuous does not survive.
Since the arrogance of base people increases all the more toward those endowed with patience,
they must be restrained by a more formidable means, so that other wicked men likewise do not act in such a way again.
When a great multitude of people, having committed a similar offense, would fall into terror at the mere apprehension [of punishment],
the lord of men should inflict the penalty at another time, under the pretext that it concerns a different matter.
Like an elephant deprived of its rut, like a serpent devoid of venom, or like a sword unsheathed from its scabbard,
a king suffers contempt if he does not inflict punishment upon those who have committed an offense.

Mortals with equal bellies, hands, and feet bow down before one [ruler] who is feared for his rod; yet they tremble even before one whose rod is excessively fierce. A rod of punishment that is commensurate with the offense leads to well-being.
Punishment for the wicked, honor for the virtuous, the lawful increase of the treasury,
impartiality toward supplicants, and the protection of the realm— these alone are declared to be the five sacrifices of kings.
Having appointed virtuous men to that [task] when fatigued, and having divided his time for the science of warfare and other matters,
the self-possessed king should perform all his duties every day in their proper order.
On every fifth day, or under the asterism of Kṣaura, or during the rising of Śmaśru or Bhasya, the king should attend to his affairs.
However, having avoided the five, seven, and three *pūrva* lunar mansions, he must not engage in travel or warfare at such times.
Established in right conduct, he enjoys the earth as far as the ocean for a long time, having uprooted his enemies.
Where there is right conduct, there is the increase of Dharma; from Dharma comes enjoyment, which he enjoys even after the dissolution of the body.
A king who is possessed of the aforementioned qualities should attack one who stands in the opposite of those stated qualities.
Having perceived that his territory or his army is impaired, or else, being free from affliction himself, he should launch an attack.
3.2ab. An army abounding in mosquitoes, lice, flies, and gadflies, or struck by a rainless shower of dust driven by the wind;
3.2cd. or one struck by a shower of flesh, blood, grain, or living creatures; or where elephants, horses, and men are oppressed and dejected.
In whose army the jackals repeatedly howl like the braying of donkeys,
having abandoned all affection for their attendants, friends, mounts, and equipment,
crying out, "Alas! Who is our refuge?"— [in that army...]
Or, if the leading men are hostile, he should be attacked by the king.
Free from laziness yet with downcast faces, they are prone to dreaming of travel;
their conduct has fallen away, their bodies overcome by the shadow of a soiled man;
sighing deeply with tearful eyes, they are overwhelmed by grief and longing.
In whose army the warriors are haters of brahmins, teachers, and friends.

He whose men in the army have their hair standing on end for no apparent reason, who have lost hope of victory, who have strayed from their natural composure, and who break into laughter at inauspicious gestures— such a person should be attacked.

He whose banners and chowries are frequented by pigeons, owls, and bees, and whose umbrellas, weapons, and other such items [are similarly occupied], or for whom the sounds of drums are not heard from his reservoirs of water—
he is to be attacked. Or else, he against whom rivers flow in reverse, or the flight of arrows [is deflected], or whose inexhaustible reservoirs of water dry up.
The appearance of water in a land where there is no water, or a stone floating upon the waters without cause—these are portents.

When the images of the gods exhibit cracking, falling, trembling, or weeping without cause; or when they remain motionless yet suddenly move, or take on the appearance of fire even without wind—these are omens.
Abnormality in childbirth, flowers out of season, wild animals entering the city,
the crowing of the cock at twilight, and the warbling of the cuckoo at the onset of winter.
If dogs bark loudly and incessantly, even out of season, with long, dejected, and huddled cries;
if women strike other women and act without compassion; or if a white crow or a rainbow is constantly seen at night—[these are signs of impending calamity].
If sesame seeds are oilless or contain only half their usual oil; if there is excessive growth of crops;
if food has a bad taste; if the sap of trees is blood-like; and if there is the withering away of thornless plants—[these are signs of calamity].
Having abandoned snakes, rats, cats, and fish, they consume the flesh of their own kind;
or else they engage in sexual intercourse with those of another species, while the birds and wild animals are constantly inflamed with passion.
The breaking and falling of arches and Indra-dhvaja banners; the reversal of cold and heat; the cracking of the earth;
the elevation of low places and the depression of high places; and the shadow of the sun moving toward the front [of the army].
If the wind blows excessively fierce for more than three days, it portends the destruction of the city known as Gandharva;
furthermore, the stars will become visible by day, while at night the entire host of stars will vanish.

The dwellings of the crows are on palaces, houses, the earth, thorny shrubs, or low ground; or they suffer from childlessness, or else they have only a single offspring. Alternatively, they draw circles upon the ground while wheeling in circles above.
By the falling of meteors, by excessive brilliance,
by retrograde or extreme retrograde motion, and by the appearance of a comet, the son of the Earth (Saturn) causes affliction through its contact with and its passage across the zodiacal signs.
Furthermore, when the [asterisms] beginning with Kṛttikā are oppressed by three [planets] each, kings are to be attacked:
the lord of Pañcāla, the sovereign of Magadha, the king of Kaliṅga, and the ruler of Ujjayinī.
The King of Ānarta, Saindhava, Hāra, Haura, the Lord of Madra, and another, the Lord of Kuraṅga—
these kings indeed suffer particular affliction for those situated in the limbs of the tortoise.
In Aṅga there was Sūrya, in the land of the Yavanas Candra, in Avantī Bhauma, and in Magadha Saumya;
in Sindhū Guru, in Bhojakaṭa Śukra, and in the region of Surāṣṭra Saura was born.
The comet appeared among the Mlecchas and was born in Kaliṅga; therefore, they are being oppressed. Since they oppress their own native lands, those regions should be attacked by the king.
Or if Tālajaṅgha and others are worshipped with blood and flesh accompanied by the loud cries of Bhairavas;
or if numerous Yātudhānas are seen—then that country, even if its prosperity has declined, should be attacked.
Whatever omens are declared to portend the ruin of a country, he fearlessly announces those very reports to the world.
Even that country to which mendicants flee after abandoning it is one where the wicked prevail.

Just as a physician makes a body that is overcome by disease or corrupted by poison firm through treatments when it is facing destruction, so does the elder (the king) make the kingdom firm through pacifying rites. The body is the treasury, the warrior is the external [force], the mantra is the [protective] charm, the enemy is the path, and life is the duration.
The mind, karma, attainment, the mantra-practitioner, and the houses beginning with the ascendant are to be considered.

The Sun, Saturn, and Mars destroy [the results of] an action, excluding the three gains (trilābha); however, the Sun and Mars do not destroy it. The benefic planets nourish it, excluding the sixth house and the setting; Venus [does not destroy it] when in the eighth or the ascendant, nor does the Moon.

Just as a king’s expedition yields the desired fruit when the lunar day, its emergence, the moon, the karaṇa, the asterism, the day, and the moment are pure [and free from malefic influences], so too does it for others;
therefore, I shall now declare this supreme secret, which one should not give to a disciple who has not resided with the teacher for a long time.
By means of yogas, kings emerge; by omens, thieves, wandering minstrels, and the like;
by the power (or qualities) of the lunar mansions, the twice-born; and by the strength of the moment, other people partake in wealth.
Just as poison mixed with medicinal substances attains a state of health through the power of their combination,
and just as clarified butter and honey, when combined, are seen to become poison;
in the same way, a planet, abandoning its own [inherent] fruit, produces results arising from its conjunction.
For this reason, I have exerted myself to speak of these various yogas.
If Jupiter is in the ascendant, Mercury and Venus are situated in the fourth house, Mars and Saturn are in the sixth house, the Sun is in the third house,
and the Moon is in the tenth house at the time of departure, that king will fully attain his desired results.
When Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, and the Sun are situated respectively in the third, sixth, eleventh, and second houses from the horā, and Venus is favorable,
one who has set out destroys even an exceedingly arrogant enemy force, just as the sun with its fierce rays destroys the darkness of night.
The sun, Yama, and the moon, when situated in the signs of Aries, Libra, and Taurus respectively,
do not become enemies when facing one another, just as lions do not face deer.
If the Sun, the teacher, is situated in the seventh house at the time of rising, and the Moon is not in the eighth house,
then the king becomes like the moon among the lotus-faces of his enemies' wives.
When Venus, Jupiter, and Mercury are situated in the second house, the Moon is in the seventh, and the Sun has entered the ascendant,
the king emerges having accomplished his purpose, having subdued his enemies like Vainateya subduing serpents.
When Venus, the Moon’s son [Mercury], and the Sun are situated in the houses of the body,
wealth, or siblings at the time of one's departure for battle, his enemies perish like moths in the fire of war.
If the Sun and Moon are devoid of strength, while the lord of the birth sign (Janmeśa) and the lord of the ascendant (Lagneśvara) are endowed with strength;
if Mercury is in the seventh house (Pātāla) or the tenth house, Jupiter is situated in the ascendant,
and Venus is positioned in any houses except the sixth, seventh, or eighth— [then that person attains prosperity].
No enemies shall stand before him at the front of battle; they will flee from him like women.
When Saturn or Mars is in the ascendant and the Sun is in the tenth house, and Venus and Mercury are in the tenth or the eleventh house,
the king— acting with cruel intent like Time itself— should march against the enemy's country to slay his arrogant foe.
If Mars and Saturn are in the houses of gain (the eleventh), enemies (the sixth), and siblings (the third), while Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter are endowed with strength,
then the earth, girt by the waters of the oceans, comes under the control of one who sets out from there.
If malefic planets are in the third house and the fourth, Jupiter is in the ascendant, and the Moon is in the seventh,
then whatever effort one undertakes will meet its destruction, just as a favor done for ungrateful people perishes.
When the Moon is in the ascendant, Jupiter is in the fourth house, Mercury and Venus are in the tenth house, the Sun is in the eleventh house,
and Saturn and Mars are in the third house, the king goes forth and subdues his enemies as if they were his own servants.
If Jupiter is in the ascendant or the Moon, with the Sun in the sixth house and Saturn in the tenth,
and Venus and Mercury situated in the fourth and fifth houses respectively, a journey brings benefits just as a mother does.
When the lord of speech (Jupiter) is situated in the ascendant, and the remaining planets occupy the eleventh and second houses for one desiring to go forth,
the enemy force is torn apart on all sides, just as Dharma is destroyed by hundreds of causes at the end of a Yuga.

In the three, the nine, and the twelfth houses, the Moon is weak; however, he who has the Moon strong and Jupiter in a quadrant (kendram), his enemies’ wives produce delightful things with their ornaments for him, and his beloveds produce delightful things for those dear to them within the army.
When Jupiter aspects [the ascendant] situated in the ascendant, and Venus is in the third, eleventh, or fourth house,
while the malefic planets are not in the second, seventh, or eighth houses— what wealth is there that one who has gone [into such a configuration] would not obtain?

If Mercury is aspected by benefics while occupying the ascendant, the sixth, tenth, or eleventh house, and the malefic planets are situated in the seventh, twelfth, or ascendant, there is no fear for the traveler; he would cross even the ocean with a stone, let alone in encounters with enemies.
When Venus, Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, and Saturn are situated in the four, three, two, one, and zero houses from the rising sign respectively,
his enemies, his strength, and the faces of women look with weariness upon his beloveds.
If Mercury is situated in the second house according to the previously mentioned yoga, and both the Moon and the Sun are established in the tenth house,
then for one who has gone there, there will be elephants arising from various forests, celebrated by the songs of swarms of bees.
If the Sun and other planets occupy the sixth, third, tenth, sixth, first, fourth, or eleventh house from Jupiter, and it is also the day of Jupiter,
then for that person who approaches the enemy's army during such a journey, destruction occurs— just as merit gained at sacred pilgrimage sites vanishes for the Mīmāṃsakas and Śravaṇakas.
If Mars, Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, and the Sun are situated in the third, the eighth, the body (the first), the seventh, and the sixth houses respectively for a person,
the hostilities of enemy armies will not persist for long, just as the conduct of worldly life does not endure when produced by wicked people.

If Mars and Jupiter occupy the sixth house, those who have gone [into exile] will attain happiness and reach their own kin; by Venus, the Sun, and Jupiter, the enemy's strength quickly goes to destruction, just as the learning of a poor man perishes through anxiety for his family.

When Venus, Saturn, Jupiter, the Moon, Mars, or Mercury occupy the ascendant, the third, the ninth, the sixth, the tenth, or the eleventh house from the ascendant— especially when Mercury is with the Sun— the secret power of the enemy is destroyed, just as it has been said that secrets are ruined among backbiters.
When a planet situated in an odd-numbered asterism from Venus, Mars, Mercury, Saturn,
or Jupiter is placed in the fourth house, the enemy of one who has departed is destroyed before long, like a servant in ill-fitting attire before his master.
If, during the journey of the preceptor of the enemies of the gods (Jupiter), he has moved into the sixth house with one intervening sign from the one situated in the *pṛṣṭha* [the eighth],
then the enemies do not laugh at the prowess of the traveler, who is like Viṣṇu with his mace raised and discus in hand.
If the five planets are situated continuously in the five houses, excluding the Sun,
and if they are positioned behind one who desires to go forth, then they cut him down like Indra cutting down his enemies.
If the son of Bṛhaspati (Saturn) and the preceptor of the great Indra (Jupiter) both simultaneously abandon their zodiacal sign during the journey,
or if Mercury and Jupiter both go to the same degree, then he shines like the king of the gods in battle.
When a retrograde planet situated in the *nistrimśa* aspect moves toward a retrograde planet,
it shall slay a king who is addicted to drink or asleep at night, provided that the ruler of that very [sign] is the *aṃśaka*.
When the Son of the Earth (Mars) and the Son of the Day-maker (Saturn) simultaneously occupy the ninth division,
then the king, having launched his assault, devours his enemies just as Tārkṣya devours serpents.
When the Moon has entered between Mercury and Venus and is situated in the fourth house (hibuka), a king—
whether departing for or entering the direction of Indra (the East)— becomes equal to Indra or Yama, or even a bringer of death.
When Venus and Jupiter are situated in the fourth house and the Moon is in the seventh,
then the king who has gone forth subdues his enemies without battle.
When the Moon has reached the fourth house and Venus, accompanied by Mercury,
is set, the husband of women attains travel and conquers his enemies in battle even without a fight.
If Venus or Jupiter, occupying the ninth-part (navāṃśa) of Mars, attains a hundredfold [strength],
it destroys the enemy's force even if it be a hundred times greater, just as poison destroys the body when it has entered the bloodstream.

When Mercury is situated more than one hundred degrees away from Mars, the army of the king who has marched there against the enemy perishes in battle; just as honor comes to an object that has been offered to a supplicant.
When the son of the Earth and the Preceptor of the Gods simultaneously enter one and the same lunar mansion,
they shall bring about the end of the enemy's army, just as the son of Droṇa did to his foes by night through a surprise attack.
When Jupiter and Mercury, or Jupiter and Venus, enter the asterism [Puṣya] together and meet there simultaneously,
then the student obtains various riches through the worship of his preceptor at an excellent sacred ford.
If another planet, endowed with strength, should occupy the fifth house from the lord of the year and so forth,
it overcomes the results declared for the rising sign and, by virtue of its own power, brings about its own specific results.
Even if Mercury alone is in a trine from Mars among the living, or the Moon from the Sun, the traveler does not go to where [the planet] has risen;
rather, whichever of those two is stronger leads him to its own destination.
He whose natal star or the star at his rising is situated in the fourth or the seventh house, and is neither aspected nor joined by benefic planets,
will— having encountered a state of wretchedness like Garuḍa encountering Śāṇḍilī— return deprived of his own strength.
If the ascendant is in the eighth house from the Hora, or in the eighth house from the natal sign,
or in an enemy sign rising from an enemy sign, or if the lords of those signs are in the ascendant, for men this is equal to consuming poison.
When the lord of the house is strong, situated in the eighth or the first house from the enemy [of the ascendant], or in the third, sixth, or eleventh house; when it is weak in the side of the enemy;
and when the lord of the direction facing away is well-placed as a directional lord (dikpati).
If one proceeds according to one's desire, one will obtain therein whatever is intended.

Benefic planets are highly praised when situated in angles (kendras) or trines; likewise, malefic planets do not bestow auspicious results in those very same positions. Even a malefic planet may certainly be employed if it is strong; however, an empty angle—[that is, the ascendant]—is not conducive to well-being.
When situated in the fourth house with both benefics and malefics, the traveler attains success only with great difficulty;
like a river among the mountain caves, it flows with falls, descents, obstructions, and bends.
When Jupiter is in the ascendant, Venus is situated in the sixth house, and the Moon is in the eighth, one who has gone forth destroys the enemy's army;
just as rain does not fall when Venus moves on its southern path, or when it is harsh or has a small body.
If Leo, Aries, Libra, Gemini, Capricorn, and Cancer are occupied by their own lords when Saturn is also in the ascendant,
the soldiers of that [king] destroy the enemy force, just as the flatteries of wandering bards exhaust the wealth of a fool.
When the rising sign is occupied by Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus, and the third house by the Sun, Saturn, and Mars for one who is departing,
his enemies do not remain firm in battle, just as the accumulated wealth of gamblers does not endure.
For those who have attained the royal yogas described in the *Jātaka*, there is an increase in sovereignty day by day;
indeed, the enemy force, like a ship on the ocean tossed by the wind, meets with destruction.
When Jupiter is situated in the ascendant and the native has malefic planets in the tenth or the eleventh house,
the king, having destroyed his enemies, returns with his limbs uninjured and attains an inexhaustible treasury.
If the benefics are in the eleventh house, the second house, or the ascendant, and the Sun is in the tenth house while Venus and Saturn are in the third or the sixth house,
his wealth and treasury increase daily through the growth of his gains, just as greed increases with the accumulation of riches.
When Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, and the Sun occupy their own signs or exaltations, or when any three of these are situated in a single ascendant,
the enemy of the king meets with utter destruction— just as a man with two wives finds happiness despite being poor.
If even a single one among Jupiter, the Sun, Mars, or Saturn is in its exaltation in the ascendant, and the Moon is in its own house, then for the person born therein,
great lineages go to utter destruction through family dissensions, just as [great trees] are destroyed by the breaking of their trunks.
If the Moon is exceedingly strong in the fourth house from the ascendant, one who has gone forth [into the world] without the strength of the Moon—
though having obtained prosperity filled with many jewels— quickly goes to ruin, just like the moon.
Those for whom benefics are situated in the ninth, fifth, and the angles (kendras), while malefics are placed in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses—
having previously bestowed wealth upon the twice-born according to rule and as deserved— they return to their own abodes with their purposes accomplished.

Starting from the east, with the seven groups of nakṣatras beginning with Aja (Aśleṣā) and ending with Bhaga (Punarvasu), moving through three revolutions, and starting from the fire-quarter (south-east), the *gama* [movement] leads to victory.

Furthermore, when the *parigha* [obstacle] is situated in the directions of wind (north-west) and fire (south-east), and has moved halfway across them, it is favorable for all directions in the nakṣatras of Maitra (Anurādhā), Aśvin (Bharaṇī), Hasta, and Guru (Jyeṣṭhā).
To the east is Indra; to the south is Ajapada and Rohiṇī, and from there the one called Aryaman—the trident (śūla).
One may proceed according to one's desire in matters concerning the afterlife, provided that one avoids these tridents even at their gates.
One who desires victory in travel should avoid the second half of the asterisms of Viśvakarman (Citrā), Yama (Bharaṇī), and the Serpents (Āśleṣā);
likewise, one should avoid the first half of those belonging to Agni (Kṛttikā), as well as Maghā and Svāti, and the entire asterism of the Thunderbolt-wielder (Jyeṣṭhā).
When a lunar mansion is afflicted by portents or malefic planets, or when it is joined by many planets,
those [planets] destroy even previously acquired wealth, just as kings of the earth (mūrttikendra) addicted to minerals [destroy the land].
The Sun, Venus, Mars, Rāhu, Saturn, and the Moon, joined by Mercury and Jupiter, are the lords of the directions in order from the front.
If [the ascendant] goes toward the lord of the direction situated on the forehead, then he falls like a tree from the bank of a river.

He who has gone to the opposite extreme of this path, and who, though possessing independent mastery, is conquered by others— he, being occupied solely with grammar, becomes an object of ridicule in the assembly of those who know poetry, as if he were merely one preoccupied with grammar.
When the sun and moon have moved by their respective courses and are situated separately during day and night,
he shines like one who knows all the sciences in an assembly of enemies, as if he were a master of all scriptures.
Avoiding the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth lunar days, as well as the *viṣṭi* and *karaṇa*, they proceed;
and then these—gold, horses, and elephants, beginning with the fourth—are the obstacles to their attainment.

He who, out of delusion, sets out on a journey when the lunar mansion or the lunar day is empty, or when it is afflicted by the *vyatīpāta* yoga, or during the *vaidhṛta* yoga— he quickly meets with destruction, like a king whose astrologer acts in opposition to his interests.
Health is obtained through the asterism (nakṣatra), wealth through the moment (kṣaṇa), and the success of one's undertaking through an auspicious lunar day (tithi).
They say that success on a journey comes through the rising of the zodiacal sign (rāśi); generally, all auspicious results [or comforts] arise from the moon (the maker of the night).

The expedition of a king who spends excessively does not shine, even if it is endowed with many virtues; it is like the wedding procession of an old man afflicted by age, though he is proud of his wealth, when Venus has vanished.
When a direction is struck by Venus, Mercury, or Saturn, or afflicted by rain during a journey, it brings low the king, just as a woman,
intoxicated with wine and agitated by passion, brings low her family by taking pleasure in another's house.

Just as one satisfied with the fruit of bark-garments and water destroys the army of enemies without hardship through those who are endowed with vigor, who are resolute, and who are noble of soul—even when the conquest of the three worlds has not yet been achieved, it destroys craving; so too does the Bodhisattva destroy the host of adversaries without affliction.
Having eaten ghee with rice mixed with sesame, or milk-rice, and having traveled eastward on an elephant, chariot, horse, or man,
enemies are unable to withstand the majesty of that king, just as young elephants cannot endure the scent of rut from a scent-elephant.
On one side are all the favorable signs, and on the other is the complete purity of the mind;
yet there may be fear in battle even for one whose heart is thus [purified], or there may be none; for even the wind is a cause of both victory and defeat.
Abounding in brave men, excellent horses, and elephants, with their kinsmen engaged in battle, these proud enemies—
when their chests are struck by the wind— go somewhere like heaps of dense cotton.
When the fragrant wind, moving favorably and clockwise, brings comfort to the body,
one who has set out [on this path] violently destroys the powers of his enemies, just as the sun destroys the darknesses.
When rebirth occurs effortlessly among grass, water, food, jewels, and garments;
Then the gate of victory for women, the earth, elephants, and horses was opened wide.

Whatever degrees of the ascendant have risen, whichever planet is situated in those [degrees] bestows the results of the ascendant; whichever [planet] has passed beyond them becomes the second [in order]. This same principle should be considered for the remaining houses as well.
Having advanced with favorable planets, fire, wind, the mind, clouds, the sound of lightning, rain, and the rainbow,
he crushes the enemy's army on the field of battle like an elephant uproots a lotus pond.
Deprived of fortune, he passes his days with great difficulty, having gone forth for the sake of intimidating others;
like one who has entered the king’s palace beyond his own power, he makes a vow out of fear of an opponent.
Endowed with divine fortune, benefiting virtuous people, and possessed of power, mantras,
and the strength of exertion, he enjoys the earth— having successfully achieved his journey— along with the Sahya, Vindhya, and Pāriyātra mountains.
If the Moon is not auspicious in its *gocara*, even if it has been purified by the *aṣṭavarga* calculation,
it will cause the destruction of results for those on a journey, like an easterly wind arising at the time of flowering.
Depending upon the strength and weakness of the Moon, the planets bestow auspicious and inauspicious results;
just as the sense organs, when joined with the mind, attain functional capacity (*karmārhatā*) and not when they are alone.
Sneezing from all directions is said to be inauspicious; the sneeze of a cow brings about death itself.
Some say that which is caused by a crane, or by an old man, one suffering from catarrh, or a child, is fruitless.

When there is an auspicious omen on the lunar day (*tithi*) and the *bha* (asterism), one who desires victory and possesses faith should set out even with a mere foot, [taking] an umbrella, a bed, a seat, and so forth.
However, if there is no purity of omen, sign, dream, or mind, then traveling for any undertaking will result in misfortune.
Likewise, if the Sun is in its own day or its own *aṃśaka*, or if the Sun has entered the ascendant at the time of departure,
it brings suffering to a man afflicted by love, or makes him devoid of wealth like a courtesan.
If [the Moon] is in its rising sign, its degree, or its day, one who has gone away will not return for long and will be dejected in mind.
Like a man of harsh nature who has obtained a young woman for the sake of pleasure, he [seizes her].
If his journey occurs during the rising of Mars, or on a day presided over by its portion, it brings imprisonment, death, or loss of wealth;
like a virtuous woman who has been courted by one blinded by passion who turns away from sin.
A journey undertaken on the days of Mercury, or during the degrees of the ascendant belonging to Mercury, brings complete satisfaction to a man;
it is like a noble woman, devoted to her lover and full of clever gestures, attending to one tormented by love.
A journey undertaken on the days corresponding to the degrees of the ascendant occupied by the Guru is auspicious; it brings about a favorable connection and fulfills one's desired wishes.
Like a wife who is pleasing to her husband’s mind, it grants pleasure and leads to the prosperity of one's lineage.
A journey undertaken on the day of Venus's *aṃśa*, *dina*, or *udaya* satisfies the traveler with various objects of desire.
Like a wanton woman afflicted by passion, she approached him who had come under the power of desire with many gestures.
A journey undertaken when Saturn occupies the ascendant or its divisions brings forth faults such as the destruction of life;
it is like a woman attached to another who, out of delusion, is pursued by one infatuated with passion.
A journey, even if endowed with other virtues, does not bring joy to the mind when it is devoid of the ascendant (lagna),
just as a woman, though well-adorned and possessed of beauty, fails to please a man if she has fallen from virtuous conduct.
The purity of the ascendant is correctly understood through omens, signs, and the inner faculty,
just as a woman's character in a foreign land is known by her conduct when she has taken refuge in undivided devotion to her husband.
A shadow, announcing auspicious and inauspicious results among humans, animals, and birds, is to be observed by those who know the signs;
it reveals the qualities of inner brilliance even from the outside, just as the light of a lamp situated within a vessel of crystal or precious gemstone.
A shadow arising from the earth that has smooth skin, nails, body hair, and head hair, and is fragrant,
brings about contentment, the acquisition of wealth, prosperity, and an increase in righteousness day by day.
Glossy, white, and green, pleasing to the eyes, such a radiance brings about good fortune, gentleness, happiness, and prosperity.
Like a mother who gives birth, this nourishing radiance bestows auspicious results upon embodied beings, generating the accomplishment of all goals.

Fierce, invincible, with the color of a lotus, gold, or fire, and endowed with splendor, prowess, and majesty—this is the Āgneyī [wind]; it leads to victory for living beings and swiftly brings about the accomplishment of one's desired goal.
A wind that is dirty, harsh, and black, smelling of evil, and rising from the northwest (anila), brings about slaughter, imprisonment, disease, misfortune, and the loss of wealth.
A wind arising from the sky that has a form like crystal, is exceedingly noble, and possesses the color of pure water, is like a treasure-trove of blessings for those endowed with good fortune.
[The deities of] the directions are Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yakṣa, and Śiva.
Furthermore, the Sun, Venus, Mars, Saturn, Mercury, the Moon, and Jupiter are the lords [of the houses].
Mahendra, who rides upon Airāvata with Śacī and carries the thunderbolt, should be worshipped— whether represented by a golden image or one made of wood—
with variegated garlands, banners, red sandalwood, and gentle offerings.
Then,
having recited the mantra "iti" before the presence of Śakra,
the king, having properly fixed Indra in his heart, should direct his assault toward the quarter of Puruhūta.
An image made of copper, representing one who possesses a thousand cows, anointed with red sandalwood paste,
honored with red garments, flowers, and banners, and adorned with sun-crystal gems.
Having first recited the *kṛṣṇa*-mantra or having performed the ritual circumambulation of the sun,
one should proceed toward the east, honoring [the deity] with milk-rice and placing the Sun and Indra at the forefront.
The body of Agni should be fashioned from gold; his banner, flower, and sandalwood paste are red.
For one desiring victory over the fire-god, the oblation is clarified butter, and the mantra to be recited is "piba" (drink).
The son of Diti (Rāhu) shall have a variegated body, or Yama may have half his body on the left side; his flowers are of various forms, and his banner is multicolored.
Having recited the mantra beginning with *śukrajyotiḥ* before him, one who desires to conquer those two—the son of Bhṛgu (Śukra) and the burner (Agni)—should set out toward that quarter.

One should worship Yama—who is made of iron, whose hand holds a raised staff, and who is accompanied by black banners, flowers, and perfumes—with offerings of sesame-rice, meat, and liquor; then the recitation of this [mantra] should be performed.

The image [of Mars] should be made with a gem known as *rudhira* (bloodstone); for Mars, there are red garlands, red banners, red sandalwood, and flowers; with offerings of cooked food and meat, one should offer praise with verses addressed to the Son of the Earth (*kṣitisuta*). Thus, having placed Yama and Aṅgāraka—the lords of the southern quarter—at the front during his departure, the king should proceed toward the south.
An image of Bhairava is fashioned on a cloth, worshipped with all kinds of perfumes, flowers, and fruits;
it is impelled by the mantra of Nirṛti and adorned with black and red flowers, banners, and garments.
The enemy of the moon (Rāhu) is made of *suradāru* wood; offerings of black flowers and other items are presented to him.
Accompanied by Nirṛti, he is honored when setting out in his own direction, and his hymn of praise and mantra have been proclaimed.
Thereafter, one should proceed to the silver image of the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), who is accompanied by his noose and the mace, and is worshipped with lotuses.
Having offered an oblation of cooked rice mixed with barley-gruel, the twice-born should praise Varuṇa with the hymn beginning "varuṇa."
The image of Saturn, made of blue glass and having a lean body, should be worshipped with black garments, garlands, and offerings.
With the mantra "Śaṃ no devī," one should set forth those two deities when going to conquer the western quarter.
The form of Vāyu should be fashioned from white clay and worshipped with white flowers, garments, banners, and so forth.
For the Lord who has set out toward the quarter of Vāyu, the mantra should be recited extensively.
The mantra for Soma is "āpyāyasva" (swell up); furthermore, [the king should wear] white [garments], garlands, and so forth.
Having placed Vāyu and Soma at the front, the king should proceed toward the quarter of Vāyu.
One should fashion an image of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) made of gold, adorned with jewels and holding a mace;
it should be worshipped with various garlands, garments, and so forth—this indeed is the mantra.
For the son of the Moon (Budha), a golden human couple is desired upon a silver seat; it should be worshipped with yellow rice, sweet-smelling flowers, and perfumes.
His recitation (*japa*) is said to be the *brahmayajña*. One should proceed toward the north, meditating on and placing the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) and Budha before oneself.
The image of Bhairava should be made of cow-hide, terrifying, and smeared with ashes; the offering (bali) should consist of boiled rice mixed with curd and accompanied by mantras.

The form of the Guru should be made of coral, wearing a pure white garment and yellow clothing and so forth, and his mantra is as follows. Having worshipped these two, one should proceed in their direction.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Quarter, their family deity, and those whose dwellings are in his city with offerings appropriate to them, he should present the *bhautika* offering.
Having prepared milk-rice, liquor, meat, minced meat, various kinds of edibles, children’s toys, fragrant flowers, roots, and sweet fruits.
Those who dwell on carriage roads, city gates, riverbanks, at crossroads, in watchtowers,
and in mountain caves or under solitary trees— those Pramathas should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
And those hosts who are the attendants of Kubera, Rudra, Ahi, Suparṇa, Śaktibhṛt, Piśāca, and Daitya;
Possessing a speed like that of the wind, proud and ever-joyful, they bear a mass of splendor that rivals the radiance of the youthful sun.
They have the faces of various birds, beasts, camels, and boars, yet they are devoid of mouths.
They are formidable, their crowns bearing fierce jewels; they are tawny like the young sun, lightning, or fire.
The sounds of falling thunderbolts and the roar of thunder, as well as the sound of one's own breathing when moving swiftly, are perceived by the mind.
And they carry iron clubs, iron bludgeons, spears, maces, illusions, staffs, axes, and *śataghnīs*.
"Having conquered our enemies, we shall return to our own realm and, through your favor, offer you double the various tributes."
"For the sake of protecting the lord of men, you must act as his allies for the destruction of the enemy forces."
"In this way, a very great service has been rendered by you; through your favor, he will accomplish the task.
Madayantikā, aśvagandhā, madanaphala, vacā, and honey are recommended [to be taken] under the first asterism and under Bharaṇī.
Siddhārthaka, bhadradāru, and vacā.
For a bath under the *kṛttikā* constellation, one should use the fragrant leaves of the *nyagrodha*, *śirīṣa*, and *aśvattha* trees;
for one seeking victory, a bath under *rohiṇī* should be performed with water containing many seeds that are praised as auspicious.
In the constellation Mṛgāṅka (Mṛgaśiras), [one should bathe] with water combined with pearls, gold, and jewels;
in the constellation Raudra (Ārdrā), with water boiled with a mixture of vacā, aśvagandhā, and priyaṅgu.
On the day of Āditya, under the Puṣya asterism, one should perform the rite with cow-dung, earth from a cow-pen, white rice,
two thousand white mustard seeds, *priyaṅgu*, and *madayantī*.

For one afflicted by a serpent, [one should bathe] with earth from a hundred anthills; for one afflicted by an ancestor (Pitrya), with the remains of offerings made to the gods; and for one under the Pūrva-phalgunī asterism, it is prescribed with salt, ghee, and young grass.
One should perform [the rite] under the *uttarā* [nakṣatras] with *śatapuṣpā*, *priyaṅgu*, and *mustā*;
under *hasta* with earth from a mountain; and under *citrā* with the remains of offerings made to the gods.

In Svāti, one should perform the rite with water-born flowers, musta-grass, lotuses, and honey; in Indrāgnī (Jyeṣṭhā), with earth from both riverbanks; and in Maitra (Anurādhā) and Mahendra (Jyeṣṭhā), with yellow orpiment and earth respectively.
On an auspicious seat, at the root [of the tree], with water and two thousand leaves made of *śamī* wood.
A bath with *dhūka*, lotus, and fish is [recommended] during the *pūrvāṣāḍhā* constellations.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should perform [the rite] with water mixed with uśīra, sandalwood, and padmaka;
in Śrāvaṇa, it is prescribed with earth from the confluence of both banks of a river and gold.
In the east (Vāsava), [incense] with ghee, bhadradāru, and honey is recommended; in the west (Vāruṇa), with ghee and honey;
in the south (Āja), śrīvāsaka and priyaṅgu; and in the north (Uttarā), fragrant substances such as aguru, padmaka, uśīra, and sandalwood are praised for the lords of men.
Under the asterism Revatī, for a man desiring to travel, [the rite should be performed] with the horns of a bull and an elephant, and with vessels filled with clarified butter and honey,
combined with yellow orpiment and collyrium, and with water.
Therefore, [one should prepare the paste] with earth from mountain-ant-hills, river-mouths, both river-banks, and the foot of Indra;
and with earth brought from the temples of elephants and bulls, from royal palaces, and from the dwellings of courtesans.
One should cleanse the crown of the head with earth from a mountain peak, and the ears with earth from an anthill;
one should wash the sides [of the body] with earth from the confluence of the two banks of a river.
From the place of Indra [the eastern gate], one should take the neck; from the tusks of an elephant and a bull, the two arms;
from the gate of the king, the heart; and from the door of a courtesan’s house, the hips.
Unbroken *māṣa* beans, steamed rice mixed with sesame seeds, and cow’s curd;
[and] the flesh of a bull and of the five kinds of wild animals, beginning with the *āśvina*.
For the [spirits] beginning with Śaṅkara, there are blood, curdled milk, rice-porridge, birds, and the flesh of serpents;
for the ancestors (Pitṛs), there is sesame-rice and *ṣaṣṭika* grain, in the two lunar mansions following that.
One should consume priyaṅgu, the flesh of variegated birds, barley-gruel, and horse-gram;
likewise, honey, clarified butter, roots, water, and even parched grain flour may be taken from the hand.
On the Śravaṇa and other [specified lunar days], one should eat rice, vegetables, and cat meat;
likewise, goat meat as desired, and groats mixed with black gram.
One should proceed to the east by elephant, to the south by chariot, to the west by horse,
and to the north by human vehicle, having given everything to the lord of each direction.
Clarified butter from the east, sesame-rice, fish, and milk— these the king should eat in clockwise order according to the direction assigned to each constellation for the sake of success.
That which is tasteless, spoiled, and infested with flies; that which is foul-smelling, causes decay, and is meager;
and that which is poorly cooked—[but rather,] that which is well-cooked, pure, beautiful, and agreeable to the mind.
At the time of departure, sweet food portends great victory.

(YY_7.22d) The sacrificial altar (*vedi*) should be auspicious, constructed according to the rules of the arts (*śulvavidhāna*), and its dimensions and location should be superior rather than deficient.
One that deviates from the prescribed measurements causes ruin, and one that is situated in a wrong direction or with a distorted shape will not grant success. (YY_8.1)

A city that is deficient on its eastern side is not desired; one that is curved toward the south is for priests (purodhas). One that is auspicious for the king's wife is in the western part; for the strength of the king, it should be in the middle of the north.
The sacrificial offering (havis) that is untouched by creatures—not even by ants, flies, or impurities—is the bestower of victory.
When the skillful domestic priest offers the full quantities of materials correctly for the sake of the kings' victory, [the rite succeeds].

When there is no breaking, forgetting, falling, or deficiency regarding the incense, garlands, sacrificial porridge, water-jars, vessels, ladles, kusha grass, fans, and clarified butter, then it shall be auspicious for the king.
If, in a peaceful direction, there should be the sounds of conchs and trumpets, or the neighing of horses and the trumpeting of elephants,
or if the joyful gestures and chatter of men are heard at the time of the fire offering, there will be victory.

The Apratiratha, the Samasta, the Yātrāliṅga, as well as the group of mantras known as Abhaya; the Svastyayana, Śarma, Varma, Aparājita, and those designated as Puṣpa (as well as those designated as Āyuṣya).
The *Indraś candraś citi* hymn, the *Candraś ca bhūtabhūta* hymn, the *Sūkta*, the *Mahāvyāhṛtis*, and those mantras dedicated to Viṣṇu and Prajāpati— these are the mantras.

Prājāpatya penances are prescribed for a king when he departs [from his palace] and when he follows after someone; I shall now describe the omens related to the fire and the domestic priest that occur at the time of the oblation.
Even when effort is exerted, the fire becomes extremely feeble; though kindled, it turns away from the wood that is to be consumed, its flames bending downward.
Its whirling crest of flame is turned to the left, it is excessively smoky, and its form flickers, dissolves, and trembles.

When the oblation offered by someone hisses and crackles, or when the fire is tawny like a rainbow or otherwise brownish-yellow (kapila), or has the hue of blood, yellow, or reddish-brown, and its form is harsh, such a fire brings about undesirable results. (YY 8.10cd)
If it resembles a dog, a donkey, a camel, or a monkey; or if it bears the terrifying form of fetters or weapons;
or if it has the smell of corpses, blood, fat, bones, or marrow; such a fire brings undesirable results and is accompanied by sparks.
The sacrificial fire, making a sound like the tearing of leather or a harsh, broken, and low drone like a frog,
and agitating the domestic priest and the members of the assembly with masses of smoke, portends misfortune.
At the conclusion of the *svāhā* invocation, the sacrificial fire, blazing of its own accord with smooth and clockwise-turning flames,
brings the earth— the mother whose beautiful necklace is the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers, and whose girdle is the ocean— under the control of the king.
Resembling a pearl necklace, a jasmine flower, or the moon, compact, bestowing pleasure upon the limbs, and of great majesty;
possessing the luster of a goad, a lotus, water, and an elephant—He, the consumer of oblations, is not sacrificed by those of meager austerity.
In the fire that resembles gold, the *aśoka* tree, a crown-jewel, coral, beryl, and a blue lotus,
no darkness finds room within the king’s palace, for it has been dispelled by the rays of the jewels.
For those whose roar— whether from their throngs of chariots, oceans, clouds, or elephants— is equal to fire or even a kettledrum,
the quarters of the sky become obscured by darkness as they travel, struck by the frontal globes of elephants blinded by rut.
When the earth— whose banners, jars, horses, elephants, and kings correspond [to the conqueror]— comes under the control of the lords of the earth,
that earth, with its Himālaya and Vindhya breasts, has its rising and setting mountains as its lower lip.
When the fire is fragrant with the ichor of elephants, parched grains from the earth, lotuses, parched rice, clarified butter, and honey,
the splendor of the king becomes as if scattered before him by the radiance of the crest-jewels of prostrate monarchs.

Whatever fruit has been described in this [chapter] regarding rites dependent on fire—such as the birth ceremonies (*jātakarma*) and other *pauṣṭika* (prosperity) rites—for all sacrifices and all fire-related rituals, one should speak thus according to what is appropriate for each.
The first asterism is that of birth; the tenth is that of action (*karma*); and the sixteenth asterism from the first is the collective (*sāṃghātika*).

The eighteenth [chapter] shall be titled "The Aggregate" (Samudāya); the third [chapter] from the twentieth [group], consisting of twenty [verses] and three [sections], shall be titled "The Nihilist" (Vaināśika).
That which is indeed the twenty-fifth is the mental [principle]; thus the entire person consists of six stars.
They say that for a king there are nine stars, including those associated with his birth, his country, and his consecration.
They desire the unadulterated lunar mansion of the king's consecration; two are common when joined with the first six.
However, in this matter, all defects and virtues depend upon one primary person.
Indeed, the planetary positions taught by Kūrma for the day of a king’s consecration are for the purpose of that consecration;
furthermore, those castes which belong to him, I shall describe their groups in due order, so that the meaning may be clear to the astrologer.

The three *pūrva* constellations together with Kṛttikā are for the elder brothers; those of the kings are the three *uttara*s together with Puṣya; and those of the farmers are the asterisms of Revatī, Anurādhā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī, as well as the lunar mansion of Prajāpati (Mṛgaśiras).
The asterisms Āditya, Hasta, Abhijit, and the two Aśvins are said to belong to the merchant class;
while Mūla, Trinetra (Ārdrā), Anila (Svātī), and Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) belong to those of fierce birth and great power.
Those whose tutelary deities are Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Aindra (Jyeṣṭhā), Citrā, or Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā) have attained the status of servants to their master.
Those born under Sārpa (Āśleṣā), Viśākhā, Śravaṇa, or Bharaṇī are designated as being of the Cāṇḍāla caste.

The Sun’s transit through the period of Saturn, when it is afflicted by the conjunction or retrogression of Mars, or when it has undergone an eclipse, or is struck by a meteor, or is oppressed by the dawn; all this is certainly inauspicious.

That [fault] is declared to be "afflicted" (upahata), or rather, it is that which arises from a perversion of the natural state (prakṛti-viparyaya). That which is corrupted by the aforementioned class of faults and characterized by the stated perversions leads to failure; [the opposite leads] to success.
When the birth asterism (janmabhā) is afflicted, there is attack by disease, loss of wealth, and quarrels;
an undertaking does not reach completion, and in a collective matter, there is internal dissension.
When the asterism of accumulation (sāmudayika) is afflicted, there is the depletion of accumulated wealth.
But when there is destruction, there arise physical calamities and mental unhappiness in the mind.
One who experiences no affliction is free from disease, partakes in happiness, possesses a robust body [and has destroyed his enemies], and is endowed with wealth.
However, one who experiences six afflictions perishes along with three others, including the lord of the earth.
Devala has declared that for one who experiences bodily affliction even without planetary afflictions,
there will be physical ruin at the end of the [karmic] ripening.
During the affliction of all [planets], one who has fasted for one day should offer oblations into the fire with the Sāvitrī mantra,
using fuel-sticks from a milk-tree, being devoted to the gods and the twice-born.
A bath with cow’s milk, white bull dung and urine,
and the leaves of the *pūrṇakośā* plant removes the sin of those who observe proper conduct when a birth-impurity occurs.
In the case of [the sin of] *karman*, one should perform an oblation of honey and ghee for ten days, abstaining from alkaline substances, liquor, and meat.
In the case of a violent assault (*sāṃghātika*) or when one is tormented by it, having abandoned meat, honey, cruelty, and sexual passion,
one should bathe (or restrain oneself), offer *dūrvā* grass into the fire, and give gifts according to one's ability.
In the case of the *sāmudayika* [demon], one should give gold and silver when the constellation is afflicted;
in the case of the *vaināśika*, one should give food, drink, and land to one endowed with virtuous qualities.

O twice-born ones, when there is mental distress, one should perform oblations with lotuses and milk-rice; the Brahmins should be honored, and one should bathe with water mixed with elephant ichor, śirīṣa, sandalwood, balā, and atibalā.
