YY_10.1ab/.One who desires to propitiate the lord of men, who is dependent upon elephants, must understand this auspicious and inauspicious [character] of elephants with diligence by means of a wise man; for the king’s victory and stability reside in his elephants. YY_10.1cd/.This auspicious and inauspicious [character] of elephants must be known with care by a learned man who wishes to serve the sovereign, since the king’s success and endurance depend upon his elephants.
One hundred and fifty cubits in length, with a width of one hundred and twenty-five,
and either square or circular— such a moat bestows an increase of elephants.
The ten fingers are broad at the base, and the ten [fingers] above are likewise; the depth of the excavation below is proclaimed to be one cubit.
The entrance should be made in the east or the north, which brings auspiciousness;
it should never, under any circumstances, be made in the south or the west.
One should not cast grass or the tip of a tree onto the ground from the height of a phallus or a pillar;
the bolt should always be joined so that it points toward the east and the north.
The door is ten [handspans] in width, and on its two sides are the *mātṛkās*;
they are fourteen handspans in height, having been set out after excluding four handspans.
There are six [creatures] situated within the perineum, and five male goats and five females;
they are buried four cubits deep, and I shall now describe their heights.
Six, seven, eight, nine, or ten finger-breadths in height, respectively;
or nine or ten finger-breadths in depth—these are the *mātṛkās* that are six finger-breadths wide.
The remaining [syllables], by the subtraction of the piercing (*vedha*), are the other *mātṛkās* in sequence;
thus is this summary of the gates (*dvārasamāsa*) proclaimed as the *vārya*.
Those with teeth like honey, well-proportioned bodies, neither smeared with filth nor emaciated, and who are patient;
those with symmetrical limbs, noble lineages equal to the gods, and auspicious hips like those of a boar.
The chest, the armpits, and the folds of skin are loose; the belly hangs down, the skin is thick, and the throat is large;
the flanks are stout along with the dark [streaks], and the gaze is like that of a sluggish lion-elephant.

Deer-like elephants (mṛga) have short lower lips, tails, and penises, and thin feet, necks, teeth, trunks, and ears; they also have thick eyes. Those with a mixture of these aforementioned characteristics are called mixed-breed elephants (saṅkīrṇanāga). A deer-like elephant has five elevations, seven cubits in length, and eight cubits in circumference.
When one, two, or three [units] are added, there arise the Mandabhadra, the Saṃkīrṇanāga, and the Aniyatapramāṇa.
The color of the Bhadra elephant is green; that of the Manda is like the color of turmeric; the Mada of the Mṛga is said to be black; and the Mada of the Saṃkīrṇa elephant is a mixture of these.

Therefore, the master builder, being purified, having observed the qualities of the ground and having performed offerings, oblations, worship of the gods, and rites of pacification, should construct the elephant stable on the southern side of the king’s palace.
The earth is crowded with *yātudhānas*, *aditis*, and serpents; it is filled with the dwellings of gods and birds situated nearby;
it is defiled by heaps of gravel, bones, and ashes; and it brings about the faults of earthly elephants.

A terrain that is slightly elevated, possessing excellent trees, inhabited by cattle, level in its center, abundant in water, free from dense thickets, pleasing to the heart and the eye, devoid of the defects of thorns, and resonant with echoing sounds— such a place is praised.
A land with trees possessing glossy sprouts and rivers flowing clockwise bestows prosperity upon one's own kingdom; furthermore, such a land is beneficial for elephants and horses.
The lands of those possessing auspicious, gentle, mixed, or tusked elephants— resembling white, red, golden, or black—
are the source of nourishment and growth for the elephants and bring fame and happiness even to the kings.
In the Jyeṣṭha, Madhya, and Jaghanya types of halls, the number of pillars is twenty-four, twenty-two, and twenty respectively;
the pillars should be twice as long as they are wide, and their height should be equal to their width.
The largest [quiver] is sixteen fingers in width, the middle one is fifteen fingers, and the smallest is less than that by one finger.
The dimensions and widths of the quivers correspond respectively to those of the staffs; their breadth is stated to be equal to half a finger.
In all the halls, the circumference of the hand-rail (kaṇṭaka) is said to be half a yoke (ardhayukta);
it is raised to the height of the hand-rail, with its base-connection secured by a firm wooden joint.
On the walls of the porch and in the windows, one should fashion decorative door-panels and lattices;
likewise, on the balconies joined with the turrets, the ornamentation described by me all around should be executed.
With pairs of lotuses, blue water-lilies, and swans, with groups of young women and flocks of birds,
and with various trees bent down by the weight of fruits, shoots, and flowers, along with parrots and bees;
It was strewn with serpents, elephants, fish, and lions, beautiful with bulbs, lotus stalks, creepers, and sprouts;
it was filled with aquatic creatures such as sea-monsters (*makara*), their forms fashioned by those skilled in the arts.
The height of the gates for elephants is incomparable; its width is that same measurement diminished by one-third.
Furthermore, the gate is diminished by one-sixth from the [width of the] hall; it is auspicious when facing either east or north.

It had a magnificent, multi-storied pavilion like a lion’s cage, with doors, thresholds, and bolts well-applied; it was adorned with beautiful pedestals, pleasing to the eye, and provided both for entry and for exit.
Candana, arjuna, śirīṣa, madhūka, devadāru, sarala, añjana, and śāla;
rohiṇī, khadira, campaka, śāka, syandana, along with kadamba and viśoka.

These trees are cool and auspicious for the purpose of binding elephants, and they promote the nourishment of the elephants; furthermore, other trees that are sturdy, excellent, and endowed with good qualities should also be used for the purpose of making pillars.
That elephant which is bound facing the east quickly displays its prowess;
such an elephant remains undefeated by kings in battles and attains a long life.
If the binding occurs while facing the southern direction, it brings about the loss of life for the elephant;
it also swiftly causes the depletion of grain and wealth for the mantra-practitioners and the lord of men.
If a serpent is caught facing west, it will always have its limbs afflicted by disease;
furthermore, it brings about the destruction of the king's wealth. Therefore, that [position] should be avoided when facing the south or the western direction.
The elephant that assumes the *bandha* posture facing north brings about the increase of wealth for its master;
it attains nourishment, long life, and invincibility in times of battle.
One who has a leftward curl, one with a horn-like protrusion, one who is crooked, one who is bent, one whose [teeth] grow in succession,
one who is pierced, one born in a cemetery, one with thick lips, one with a humpbacked torso, and one who is deficient in limbs— [these are to be avoided].
A large knot that is crushed by the thunderbolt brings about inauspicious results;
all such [knots] serve for the binding of the *nāgas*. Therefore, I shall now declare their fruits.
After six months, having reached a bond upon a pillar with an upward hole,
the elephant, oppressed by a wind-disease, meets his death.
If pierced in the *koṭara*, the serpent dies; if in the *kolākṣa*, it shall incur blindness.
If pierced in the *granthicita*, it suffers from the pain of hunger; if at the tip of the *śūla*, it meets death by the spear.
In the case of those who are deficient at the root, the tip, or are hunched, death occurs within a year along with that of the female elephant;
in the case of one with a horn-like growth, death results from honey-poisoning, and in the case of one afflicted by worms, death results from disease.
When the creeper is corrupted, there is a breaking of the body; when it is scattered over the nose, and when it curls to the left, all the mounts of the king perish.
When it is within the earth and is called *kuṇila*, it leads to the death of the king along with his great subjects.
But for a nāga, capture occurs when it is at a triple-bend, or during combat against a pillar.
An elephant that is born after [the mother], pierced, or bound, or one that is delicate, meets with death;
for one born in a cemetery and bound, death occurs within two years.
If the lines at the tips of the trunk are thick, the great elephant dies in the eighth month; if it is bound in a place abounding in pits, it suffers from the affliction of hunger.
A large knot [on the trunk] causes death by boils for elephants in their second year;
if struck by lightning, the death of the elephants should be known to occur within six months.
Pillars free from defects and pure lead to victory; they bestow strength and nourishment upon elephants.
From the point where the two ear-threads intersect, one should measure out one and a half cubits; there,
in the northeast direction, a pillar should be erected for the purpose of tethering elephants, for the welfare of the king and his tuskers.
In the southeast, there is death to elephants and loss of wealth from the king; in the southwest, defeat in battle and destruction of property;
in the northwest, disease occurs to the elephant; therefore, it should be planted in the northeast for prosperity.
The best [stūpa] is ten cubits high, the middling is nine, and the smallest is said to be eight cubits in height.
All should be buried four cubits deep; if they exceed or fall short of these measurements, they will not lead to auspiciousness.
The width at the base should be twenty finger-breadths, decreasing successively by two, three, and four;
indeed, those same measurements at the top should be reduced by two, and the circumference around the edge should be three times that.
They have copper-colored lips, palate, and faces; eyes like those of the *kalaviṅka* bird; smooth and prominent upper teeth; and broad, elongated mouths.
Their chests are high like a bow, with well-concealed and deeply set spinal columns; their slender shoulders are covered with a single hair and resemble the shell of a tortoise.
Those with broad ears, jaws, navels, foreheads, and private parts; those with nails numbering eighteen, twenty, or twenty-two, and raised like the shell of a tortoise;
those whose hands are rounded and enriched with three lines;
such men are strong, fortunate, and possess breath from their lotus-like mouths that is fragrant and intoxicating.
Elephants with long fingers, red lotus-like trunks, and a roar like that of a water-laden cloud; possessing large, long, and rounded necks—such are the elephants of a king, considered auspicious.

Those whose nails, limbs, and body parts are devoid of luster, or who are superior, inferior, or deficient; those who are hunchbacked, dwarfed, or have horns like a ram; those whose bellies, fruits, or faces appear wretched; and those whose palates are dark brown, blue, variegated, or black—[these are not to be accepted].

A king shall send away to a foreign land those with very small mouths, those with hair growing on their palms, lepers, eunuchs, female elephants, and even a pregnant elephant endowed with the marks of a male elephant; these yield extremely inauspicious results.
Having measured twice the circumference and length of the root of the tooth, one should fashion it beyond that;
if it appears dark-brown, dusty, or blood-stained, and resembles a wicked being, it brings misfortune.

When a mark appears on a fashioned tooth, having the form and appearance of a royal insignia, then there is prosperity, victory, wealth, and increase in power; such marks are auspicious when they are glossy, white, and beautiful.
In the south, there is extreme auspiciousness; it is exceedingly beautiful. In another direction, even evil is extremely deformed.
When that is reversed, it becomes fit for recitation; this detail has been proclaimed by other sages.
The gods, Daityas, and humans are situated respectively at the base, the middle, and the tips of the teeth;
consequently, the fruit is abundant, middling, or very slight, and arises quickly, after a moderate time, or after a long period.
Regarding the result of a broken tooth here: if it is on the right side, it brings about the flight of the king, the country, and the army;
if on the left, it causes fear for the son and the domestic priest, and destroys servants, wife, and leaders.
One should predict the total destruction of the king's lineage upon seeing signs of a double failure;
through gentle ascendants, lunar days, and asterisms, auspiciousness increases, and otherwise, the opposite occurs.
If there is milk, or trees with desirable fruits and flowers, or the sound of splashing against the banks of a river;
or if there is a fracture or breaking of the left or middle teeth—these portend the destruction of enemies; otherwise, the opposite occurs.
With a stumbling gait, his ears suddenly bristling with alarm, he is exceedingly dejected and pants softly yet very deeply, resting his forelegs upon the ground.
With eyes rapidly blinking, prone to sleep, contrary, and causing fear, he eats unwholesome things; repeatedly, he voids blood and excrement.

If an elephant, with a joyful gaze, moves at its own will along the direction of the expedition, lifting its trunk high and walking with quick steps, crushing anthills, stumps, thickets, sugarcane, and trees;
and if it repeatedly sprays water from its temples or trumpets loudly, it portends victory.
Or at that time, the attainment of the Madāpī yoga brings victory; likewise, the right [hand] bringing the tooth to the lips does so as well.
The elephant entering the water to be seized by a crocodile portends the destruction of the king;
whereas the elephant seizing the crocodile and crossing from the water onto dry land brings prosperity to the lord of men.
In battle, the royal fortune of kings belongs to those who conquer their enemies;
victory belongs to those whose excellent elephants have temples stained with rut. A single intoxicated elephant shatters the enemy host, which is thick with other maddened tuskers.
Therefore, I shall now describe the collection of substances that removes the rut of elephants.
Of *jātī*, *guḍūcī*, *kadalī*, sesame, *āsphota*, cotton, and *balā*;
and of *mārgī*, *nīlī*, *girikarṇikā*, *dhattūra*, *syandana*, and *māṣa*—these are the constituent parts.
Kalambukā, karṇaka, āpaparṇī, punarnavā, bhṛṅgaraja, aśvagandhā, śephālikā,
soṭaka, kacchurā, kośātakī, gokṣuraka, and vidārī.
Viṣṇukrāntā, dugdhikā, śālaparṇī, khaṭvāpādī, vākucī, vastagandhā,
vyāghrī, pṛṣṇiparṇī, mṛṇāla, paṭoraka, sallakī, and taṇḍulīya.

When these [qualities] are combined as appropriate, there is an increase in the rut of the elephant in rut; for one who is free from intoxication, there is the joy of giving, beauty in every limb, and an exceeding radiance in the face.
And the roots of *Saubhāñjana*, *Nimba*, *Iṅguda*, and *Paruṣaka*.
The roots of śatāvarī, kākolī, and the two types of kṣīrakākolī;
the roots of śleṣmāntaka, śālmali, and śallakī; and likewise those of bimba—these should be used.
Kāśī, śyāmāntaka, and the roots of rājamāṣa—
these all always produce a beautiful luster for the mouths of elephants.

A bolus made of powdered *māṣa* beans mixed with curd and crushed indigo leaves, prepared with buffalo milk, quickly brings about the onset of rut in the lords of elephants; indeed, indigo alone is the preeminent substance among all such preparations.
Indeed, *kākajaṅghā* alone acts [as a purgative], as do *māṣaparṇī* and *mudgaparṇī* each individually;
likewise, *tāmbūlavana*, fresh *vṛścikālī*, and *mustā* are each individually intoxicating.
One should know that either a single cotton plant joined with *cañcu*, or a single thorny plant called *śailikā* [is used];
likewise, a single bark of *sphūrjaka* is praised, or *kuṭhera* combined with *bhṛṅga* and *jātī*.
In the same way, the root of the *iṅgudī* tree causes an abundance of rut;
and there is one white *kāmbojī*, and another white *aparājitā*.
The clump of *vīraṇa* grass with its roots, as well as the jasmine with its roots,
and even the blue lotuses, produce an abundance of fragrance through their intoxicating essence.
Surasā combined with gaṇḍa, or punarnavā, or cow dung, should be steamed;
likewise, the roots of vārāhī mixed with jaggery are praised.
Sugar mixed with honey provides a beautiful luster to the mouths of elephants;
a bolus of molasses is beneficial for those whose diet consists of sugarcane products, and one mixed with curd is likewise beneficial.
For those who eat black gram (*māṣa*), [clarified butter] mixed with molasses is recommended; for those who eat grass, it is recommended when combined with fat (*vasā*).
For those whose diet is mixed, one should administer it after having ascertained their relative strength and weakness.
Generally, wind (vāta) causes the destruction of intoxication (mada); therefore, one should frequently apply to it boluses mixed with ghee.

One should cause it to sweat, so that there may be an increase in intoxication; and for one whose intoxication has broken off, one should administer remedies that promote the increase of intoxication. One [who is fit] has a long neck, eyes, and forehead; a broad triple-joint (trika) and heart; and copper-colored palate, lips, and tongue.

A horse with fine skin, hair, and tail; with well-formed hooves, gait, and mouth; with short ears, lips, and tail; with rounded shanks, knees, and thighs; with even and white teeth; and possessing a beautiful form and proportions—such a horse, pure in all its limbs, always brings about the destruction of the enemies of the king.

If the fire is emitted from the wrong side, it does not bring good fortune; likewise, if it stays on the other side of the seat or flares up on the left, it is unfavorable. Therefore, the opposite is praised. Flaming from all limbs brings no increase for horses, nor do sparks or smoke for two years.

When the fire blazes in the private parts, the harem goes to ruin; when it blazes in the belly, there is depletion of the treasury. If it blazes in the anus or the tail, there will be defeat; but if it blazes in the mouth or the head, there is victory.
The blazing of the shoulders, the seat, and the limbs is prescribed for victory; the blazing of the feet is taught for the purpose of binding.
Smoke appearing on the forehead, chest, eyes, and arms leads to defeat, whereas their blazing leads to victory.
If the nostrils, the muzzle, the head, the shedding of tears, or the eyes blaze at night, it leads to victory.
It is always auspicious for horses that are the color of *pālāśa* flowers, copper-colored, black, brindled, or white like a parrot.
Hostility toward fodder and water, sweating without a cause, trembling,
or the spitting of blood from the mouth, or the emergence of smoke;
sleeplessness at night and excessive drowsiness during the day while in meditation— these are signs of contradiction.
Sinking down and having a downward gaze—this movement of horses is considered undesirable.
Mounting another horse, or a horse already equipped with a saddle and gear, or even riding a noble steed that is untrained— such actions are not auspicious.
Like cranes, they neighed for the slaughter of the enemy with unwavering necks and uplifted faces;
the horses neighed affectionately, loudly, and resonantly like joyful beings, their mouths as if filled with morsels of food.
A full vessel, curd, a brahmin, a deity, perfumes, flowers, fruit, gold, and so forth;
or whatever other desirable object there may be—if [the horse] neighs when near these, there will be victory.

Horses that delight in fodder, drinks, and grain, or who rejoice at the master’s approach; or those whose gaze is directed toward their left flank, or who grant the fruits of the desired object—such are the horses.
If they strike the earth with their left feet, it portends the departure of their master;
if they neigh while looking toward a blazing twilight, it forebodes captivity and defeat.
Those that neigh excessively, scatter dust over fools, and speak while fond of sleep;
those that are hairless, have a weak and harsh voice, are tall, and swallow [their own food]—these are portended for fear.

Those who stand with their right side turned toward the sun, lifting their right foot as if holding a casket, [indicate] victory; the wise man should likewise predict this result according to its possibility even for the remaining mounts.
When a king who is endowed with discipline mounts another horse that follows him on his journey and neighs toward it,
or if the horse touches its own right flank with its muzzle, that horse will soon increase the prosperity of its master.

If a horse, even when being struck, repeatedly voids urine and dung and does not move in the proper direction, and if it is fearful of what ought not to be done and has tearful eyes, that horse does not bring prosperity to its master.
A sword measuring fifty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) is the best; it may be as little as twenty-five.
A wound located at the measurement of one finger-breadth (aṅgula) from the joint should be known as auspicious.
Wounds resembling banners, weapons, and svastikas are praised when they are symmetrical.
On a sword, wounds that follow the grain and are numerous do not bring good fortune.

That which is cracked, short, blunt, or broken like a bamboo, as well as that which is not followed by the eye and mind, is called "toneless" (asvara) and is undesirable; the opposite of what has been described yields the desired fruit.

The ringing of [the sword] is said to portend death; its failure to emerge from the scabbard indicates defeat. When it emerges of its own accord, there is battle; when it blazes forth, victory is attained.
One should not display it without cause, nor should one strike it; one should not look at its face, nor speak of its price.
One should not disclose its location, nor should one honor it; and the king, being unpurified, should not touch the sword-blade.
It has the shape of a cow’s tongue, resembles the petal of a blue lotus or a bamboo leaf,
is like the leaf of the *karavīra*, has a tip like the lunar disc, and is praised.
Once completed, it cannot be cut; it must be made according to the prescribed measurements.
When [the image] dies, the master dies; when its mother is cut off before it, [the master dies].

In whatever part of the hilt there may be a wound, that same [mark] belongs to the sword; it should be described as being on the face [of the sword], just as a *tilaka* on the private parts of women is seen on their faces.
Alternatively, having determined which limb the questioner touches while holding a sword,
one who knows this science of swords should indicate the wound as being located within the scabbard.
When the head is touched at the first finger-breadth, at the second there is contact with the forehead;
at the third it is between the eyebrows, and at the fourth the eyes are touched.
The first five [vital points] are located in the nose, lips, cheeks, jaw, ears, and neck;
the twelfth is situated in the chest, and the thirteenth is to be known as being in the armpits.
In the breasts, heart, abdomen, flanks, and navel, the fourteen [ribs] and so forth are to be known;
at the base of the navel, the hips, and the private parts, there are nineteen [vertebrae].
In the twenty-second [digit] from the thighs there would be a wound; in the middle of the thighs, in the twenty-third;
at the knee, in the twenty-fourth; and on the calves, it would be in the twenty-fifth.
In the middle of the shanks, at the ankles, on the heels, in the feet, and also in the toes—
from the twenty-sixth up to the thirtieth [day], according to the opinion of Garga.
The death of a son, the acquisition of wealth, the loss of wealth, prosperity, and slaughter—
these results should be indicated in sequence by means of wounds located at intervals of one finger-breadth and so forth.

The gain of a son, quarrels, the acquisition of an elephant, the death of a son, and the gain of wealth; then, in sequence, destruction, the attainment of a wife, and mental anguish—these occur starting from the sixth [year].

Gain, loss, the triad [of gain, loss, and stability], death, growth, death, and contentment—these fourteen results should be known for the first [houses] and so forth; and there shall be loss of wealth in the twenty-first.
The attainment of wealth, non-extinction, the arrival of riches, death, prosperity, and lack of ownership;
sovereignty, death, and kingship—these constitute the sequence up to thirty.
Beyond that, there is no superior fruit; those situated unevenly or evenly yield results that are evil or auspicious.
Some have declared them to be fruitless beyond thirty, up to the maximum limit.
It brings auspicious results and has an odor like cow urine, yellow orpiment, mud, or fat.
A scent resembling the fat of a tortoise, or like stale alkali, brings fear and suffering;
whereas one with the luster of lapis lazuli, gold, or lightning brings victory, health, and prosperity.
This sword-drinking ritual of Aiśānasa, performed with blood for one desiring blazing prosperity;
and this offering of potent oblations for one wishing for a daughter, and the desire for inexhaustible wealth through water—[all these are futile].
If one desires the accomplishment of an objective through evil means, it is like drinking the milk of a mare, a camel, or a female elephant.
For the purpose of severing the trunk of an elephant, one should use the bile of a fish, the milk of a deer, a horse, or a goat, combined with *sātala* seeds.
A plaster consisting of the milk of a *arka* plant, mixed with the soot from a rhinoceros horn and the dung of a pigeon and a rat, [should be applied].
Then, by drinking oil that has been churned from this [iron], and subsequently having it tempered with *śrī* (honey), there shall be no damage to the blade upon striking stones.

Iron that has been soaked for a day in an alkaline solution mixed with *kadandī* and stirred with buttermilk, when properly tempered upon a stone, does not break; nor does it lose its internal toughness even when struck against other metals.
Whether from the inner apartments, from his own residence, from the lion throne, or from the sacrificial fire-altar—
The lord of men should first set out on his journey after having had auspicious blessings conferred upon him by hundreds of eminent brahmins.
The twice-born should cause [the disciple] to take further steps with the Viṣṇu-strides by means of this mantra;
he should lift up his foot with the words, "Viṣṇu strode through this."
"‘For the slaying of so-and-so,’ thus the king should place [the mantra] on the right [side].
Then, beholding, touching, and hearing auspicious things, the king should proceed. (Kane V. 621; YY_13.3)
The treatises on Dharma and Artha, the Mahābhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa, and hymns of auspicious praise.
Auspicious sounds were heard from cranes, blue jays, peacocks, kadamba ducks, swans, and jīvajīvaka birds;
there was a crow upon the back of a boar smeared with mud, as well as śrīvṛkṣa trees, yak-tail fans, and sandalwood.

A cow fond of her calf, a goat, a rucaka gem, priyaṅgu seeds, parched grain, chariots yoked with men, banners, all medicinal herbs, svastikas, full vessels, a horse, and then dūrvā grass, red radish, and cow dung.
The lakes that cannot be dried up, the rivers, oceans, Rudras, Indras, world-protectors, mountains, and nāgas;
the quarters, planets, constellations, Śiva, Suparṇa, Skanda, Viśākha, the Maruts, and the Sādhyas.
The earth, the twelve suns, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins; Svāhā, Śacī, the host of Mothers, and Bhavānī;
the wives and mothers of the gods and asuras, the Sādhyas, the Apsarases, and the Vidyās.
May the yakṣas together with the siddhas, the sages with their wives, the rain-clouds, earthquakes, trees, and winds,
as well as Prajāpati and the omnipresent Viṣṇu, be for your welfare, O King, upon your journey.
White mustard seeds, a mirror, milk, and ointments; a bound single animal, meat, and a full water-jar;
curd, honey, ghee, yellow pigment (rocanā), a young girl, a banner, gold, a lotus, an auspicious throne, and a conch shell;
a white bull, flowers, and garments; a pair of fish, a flock of birds, a courtesan, and beloved people dressed in beautiful attire.
Flaming crests, fruits, seeds, unbroken grains, and parched rice; elephants, clay drums, goads, fly-whisks, and weapons;
emeralds, rubies, and sapphires; and various kinds of jewels, foremost among them crystal and mani-gems.
Whether auspicious signs are produced spontaneously or recounted without effort,
he conquers the entire earth by means of those [signs] being attended through their striking, appearance, touch, and sound.

Cotton, medicinal herbs, black grain, salt, eunuchs, bones, oil, fat, mud, charcoal, molasses, snakes, hides, excrement, hair, those afflicted by disease, the shaven-headed, those who have smeared themselves [with ashes],
those with disheveled hair, the fallen, and those wearing saffron robes— all these portend inauspiciousness.

One should proceed along a path where the sound of sharp-sounding drums, clay drums, conchs, kettledrums, and lutes resounds, which is adorned with banners and the tops of archways, where the dust is laid by abundant flowers and water, and where the people are fragrant and well-attired.

Whatever auspicious or inauspicious signs have been prescribed here for those departing, these same favorable or unfavorable omens apply even to dreams; likewise, being smeared with excrement is auspicious.
The chuchundarī, the sow, the jackal, the śyāmā, the ralā, the piṅgalikā, and the cuckoo;
the female house-lizard and those birds designated as male are auspicious when on the left.
The hawk, the ruru deer, the pūrṇakuṭa, the monkey, the śrīkarṇa, the chikkāraka, the pippika, the goat,
those known as female, and the peacock and elephant— these are beneficial when situated on the right side during travel.
Crows on the left at the time of departure bring good fortune to men, while their crying on the right portends misfortune for others.
The peacock, the partridge, the blue jay, and the mongoose bring auspiciousness through their cry and their sight;
the lizard brings good fortune when seen crying out.
The iguana, the boar, the mongoose, the snake, the hare, and the lizard are auspicious when heard or seen making sounds.
The recitation of this [chapter] is auspicious; its fruit is like that of the bear and the monkey, and it is excellent when applied in reverse.
For the mongoose, the deer, and birds, moving from the left to the right side is auspicious;
for the dog and the jackal, this same movement is praised as having the opposite result.
The blue jay and the mongoose, when moving to the left after midday, bestow auspiciousness;
likewise, dogs in the forests behave like deer, and the woodpecker is auspicious on the right at sunset.
Regarding the loss of things, the sight of them, their reunion, the sequence of battles, entering houses, and the sight of younger brothers or lords,
some authorities have declared that certain [auspicious] results occur through the reverse method of travel, just as in the case of the sight of kings during journeys.
Situated among trees that are undamaged and pleasing to the mind, and established upon pure, beautiful ground and vegetation;
even one that yields inauspicious results is declared to bestow auspiciousness when [constructed] during times of favorable lunar days, days, asterisms, and ascendants.
In places where trees are broken or withered, among thorns, or which are strewn with cemetery ashes, bones, and chaff;
and in ruined walls or desolate dwellings that are difficult to behold—even an auspicious omen is declared to be evil.
The direction facing the sun is "charcoal-colored" (aṅgāriṇī), and that in which the sun stands is "blazing" (pradīptā).
That toward which the lord of day will move is "smoky" (pradhūmitā); the remaining directions are "calm" (śāntā) and they shall bestow auspicious results.
When the [direction] has been released, it should be known as "gone"; when it is blazing, it is "present"; when it is smoky, it is "to come," which is undesirable.
When the five directions other than those [three] are thus extinguished, [the result] is imminent; for the remaining two, it is "extinguished-blazing."
One who eats meat and impure food is naturally fierce, while one who eats grass and fruit is naturally peaceful;
both types are thus described as eaters of food. Furthermore, they should be considered according to the direction, place, rising sign, and time.
Those afflicted by dualities, chronic diseases, or fear; those intoxicated, distressed, or engaged in war; those desiring meat;
and those separated by boundaries or rivers—all these should not be considered as yielding either good or bad results.
An empty jar, when raised for the purpose of fetching water, brings success on a journey;
it is especially so for those seeking knowledge, those intent on theft, and those striving in mercantile activities.
The blue jay, the *andīraka*, the wagtail, the parrot, the crow, the three kinds of pigeons,
the *bhāradvāja*, the *kulāla*, the cock, the donkey, the harpy, the vulture,
the monkey, the *pheṭa*, the dog, the *pūrṇakūṭa*, and the sparrow are said to be those that roam during the day.
The hairy one (*lomāsika*), the one called the tawny six-legged insect (*piṅgalachappikā*), the flying fox (*valgulī*), the owl (*ulūka*), and the hare (*śaśaka*)—
if all these wander out of their own proper time at night, it portends the destruction of the king or his subjects.
The spotted deer, the jackal, the porcupine, the myna bird, the cat, the crane, and the boar—these are [auspicious] both by day and by night.
Those planets that move both by day and by night, which travel through cities and forests at their own time and remain in their own domains, are fruitful;
those situated in the opposite positions are fruitless. These are inauspicious for one desiring to go to a city or for a king.
A carriage has fallen with its pole, a large maiden stands before me with an exceedingly great womb, and voices cry out, "Come!
Stay! Enter! You are going—why? These sounds, though steady, forbid my departure.
Indeed, Gāndhāra, Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, and Madhyama are the auspicious notes for a vehicle, but not those that remain here;
the gods also desire the two auspicious scales known as Madhyama and Ṣaḍja, as well as the Gāndhāra song.
In all circumstances, they declare a sneeze to be an omen of evil; however, a cow's sneeze portends death for one who is about to depart.
Furthermore, the meowing of a cat, a stumble, and the tearing of one's garment are not auspicious signs for a traveler.
A water-jar and a horse-herd’s hand are not auspicious when situated in the east; nor are a killer and a weapon-bearing hand when situated in the direction of Yama (the south).
Furthermore, a eunuch and a liquor-maker in the west, along with a seat, a plow, and a threshing floor, bring water.

White objects and a horse are most excellent in the east; a corpse is equally auspicious in the south; a young girl and curd are highly praised in the west; and cows, Brahmins, and virtuous people are excellent in the north.
That which has a full crest and is called *sakarāyika* is auspicious when on the left in the eastern region;
the crow is auspicious on the right in those [regions], while in other regions it is the opposite.
On the left side, an elephant of the Dhanvana type is auspicious and a bestower of success if it is very tall and measures one cubit;
if it is tall in its body and on the left side, the Dhanvana elephant brings the acquisition of land.
If it urinates while moving ahead of the traveler, then the king shall destroy the enemy force.
If a dog goes toward poison, thorny bushes, dry trees, clods of earth, bones, or rags,
or if it barks facing the traveler while shaking its head, fighting, scratching the ground with its claws, or vomiting, it is not auspicious.
The wicked man sleeps with his feet turned upward, and upon seeing the sun, he cries out piteously;
one who is intent on obtaining dry bones is miserable, whereas one whose mouth is full of meat and the like is auspicious.
If a blue jay with a full face makes a clockwise circle or a svastika in the sky, there will be great gain for him;
after a time, his defeat leads to victory, and he attains triumph.
If a primary omen occurs during an intermediate one, one should know that the result will certainly be obtained on that very day; thus these matters are to be considered.
Likewise, at the time of commencing a task or embarking on a journey, as well as upon entering [a house], they maintain that a sneeze occurring at such times is never auspicious.
Some say that the cry of a bird beyond the distance of one *krośa* is fruitless; however,
if an inauspicious first omen occurs there, the king should perform five or six *prāṇāyāmas*,
and likewise sixteen if the second omen is unfavorable.
If the third [alternative] is undesirable, one should return from there to one's own abode.

They say that for a king who honors [the astrologer], there will be auspicious results from the ripening of the planetary periods, success without obstacles, protection of one's fundamental assets, or the acquisition of allies; and for one who is wicked, they predict total ruin and disease.
Those born of great families of heroic warriors, devoted to their master, powerful, and well-trained, [are the ones to be employed].
Those with visible marks have many kinsmen and friends; their arms are like the trunks of *nāga* trees, and their limbs are firm.
Those who have the roars of tigers, lions, bulls, and oxen; whose eyes are like those of hawks and whose noses resemble those of parrots;
and whose eyes are squinting, crooked, or closed—these are the companions of those who perform meritorious deeds in battles.
There were many leaders, renowned for their virtues as men of the land, distinguished by the marks of excellence;
they were supported by the state, their faces contorted with frowns, and they bore various weapons in their hands.
The staff and serpent belong to Saturn; the discus to the Sun; the lotus and the cart to Venus; and the eagle to Mercury.
The needle and the hand-formation belong to Mars; the hawk to Jupiter; and that called the circle to the Moon as well.
That which is an array of one's own auspicious planets, or of those of enemies situated in inauspicious positions,
or that which is employed against an enemy’s configuration— this is the means of destruction by enemies who possess superior strength.
When battle is imminent, the king, having consulted with his ministers,
should exert force and energy that causes the enemy host to flee;
for the astrologer declares victory, and the people speak the truth.
And there were auspicious omens for me regarding the elephants, horses, warriors, and so forth.
"You are of noble birth, and people speak of your prowess;
you have applied yourselves to the bow, the javelin, the discus, and the spear. Since you possess such affection for me, why should victory not be mine?"
When this world, with its elephants and horses, shall be trampled underfoot by you, [then you will attain liberation].
The elephants, horses, Brahmins, fires, enemies, and warriors roar, neigh, utter auspicious words, blaze, and shine, filled with joy; what doubt can there be regarding victory in this battle?
The laws that were proclaimed by the Sage who is the path of aversion and by Manu for battles are indeed known to you.
For those who sacrifice their bodies for the sake of their master, cows, twice-born ones, or for what is beneficial, worlds are easily attained and victory is vast.
That goal which is attained only after a very long time by ascetics through strenuous effort, and by those performing sacrifices with the three fires—
that destination the wise attain swiftly, having become the sacrificial victims in the horse-sacrifice of battle.
For one whose austerity people do not speak of, nor his death in battle, nor his victory,
nor his great wealth consisting of learning and generosity— his existence is equal to that of a worm or an insect.
Even while being guarded, this body will inevitably meet its destruction, having abandoned friends, sons, and wealth.
Therefore, what is better: to speak boastfully in the presence of friends, or to slay an enemy army with a frowning face?

Crying out "O father! O mother! while tormented by pain, wallowing in his own excrement, urine, and phlegm—would it not be better for him to be dead than to be thus in his home, or what of him in battle with his mouth terrifying as his lips are bitten?
Let the rest of the world remain auspicious for now; as for those men who turn their backs in battle, even their wives do not look upon their faces before their friends out of shame.
I shall describe that happiness which comes from advancing after having shattered the enemy host—
the happiness of those who hear the sharp sprouts of their own fame serving as ear-ornaments for the faces of the women who are the quarters of the sky.
A lion falls upon the head of an elephant, whose body is a mass of flesh exceeding a hundred times its own size;
it drinks that blood, which has a scent like liquor, and slowly swallows the pearls that have been released from its mouth.
Young women adorned with jewels and gold, elephants, horses, wealth, and the breeze of yak-tail fans;
a parasol with the luster of the constant moon—these do not belong to one who is fearful of battle and whose face is turned away from his mother.
Seated upon celestial chariots, the wives of the gods— won through battle— take great delight with intense joy as the fawn-eyed women press their noble thighs against the radiant cage of his arms.
On one side, the host of celestial beauties and Fortune welcome him as he desires to fight; on the other side, his fame flees along with Lakṣmī, while his family’s disgrace remains behind.
The gardens, temples, wells, tanks, and sacrifices that you have established, as well as the pleasures you have enjoyed through the favor of the king—
all those will be in vain if your sword does not flash like a streak of lightning in the midst of battle without fail.
"Tell me, what is so wonderful or what is such a rash act in this, that they would not spare their own lives for the sake of their master?
That you, O fool, having escaped from battle, remain here known to be in the midst of the enemy—that indeed is a rash act."
Not only are the wounds inflicted upon a hero’s limbs in battle his ornaments;
those very wounds that scar the roots of the tree of fame are the true ornaments of his lineage.
When the warriors have been broken, those who were engaged in battle— having filled their weapons and been deprived of life—
now gaze upon the celestial chariots of those who, with faces turned upward, have attained the world of the Horse Sacrifice.
Whatever fruit has been declared by the gods, the twice-born, or the authors of the Vedic scriptures for the horse-sacrifice,
that very same fruit is prescribed at every step for one who proceeds in reverse order through its stages.
Many paths to heaven have been taught; they are difficult to accomplish, circuitous, and beset with obstacles.
But this path—attaining the state of a hero in battle—is straight and yields great fruit in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Having witnessed the sovereignty [of heaven] for those who, having encountered battle, have given up their lives for the sake of their master, cows, or Brahmins,
people desire birth again very quickly out of greed for victory, even though they have earned the heavenly world through arduous means.
Fainting from the blows of combat, they see themselves as if waking from sleep,
resting in the laps of celestial nymphs whose limbs are fanned by the breezes of the Mandākinī.
Whether he is alive or slain in battle, for a man fighting there is indeed only dharma;
for by his resolve in combat, he does not die at all, being never subject to fear, old age, or death.
Even an insect, a bird, or a beast fights by relying on pride alone;
what man indeed would abandon a battle that bestows heaven, happiness, fame, and wealth?
"That which has ceased to be does not exist for me anywhere; that which is to be, whether existent or non-existent, where will it go for me?
Having reflected thus, the wise enter the enemy armies undaunted.

Pressing their breasts firmly against the jeweled slabs of the altar with their chests, and leaning on their arms as they stand upon the sacrificial ground, the celestial women dwelling in their mansions in the sky cry out, "Alas!
Alas! Others, hurrying through side-gates, wail aloud; thus the world of the gods carries away the slain from the front of the battle by the swiftness of their hands.

Slain in battle, they enter headlong into the celestial chariot— which is filled with swans, where the hollows of its jeweled pedestals are infested with serpents, which serves as a garment for its pleasure-gardens, which has golden griffins set with variegated gems upon its turrets, and which features lions perched upon its pillars— resembling the rising sun.
In this context, banners and weapons consecrated with mantras effect the destruction of enemies and the defeat of hostile armies.
The Blessed One Uśanas proclaimed the mantra in his own treatise; that which is written here follows the sequence of the preliminary rites as previously described.

With a steady heart, one should easily destroy the enemy force that has approached with elephants, horses, and heroic warriors in agitation, with weapons raised against him, and facing the radiance of the sun.
If an inauspicious bird or beast alights on his right side like a banner of the comet,
or if the sound of his musical instruments is indeed harsh, discordant, dull, and ragged on his left side;
When the enemy army has its archers, elephants, horses, and warriors stationed at the rear in a formed array,
and a rainbow appears fixed upon its forehead, a skilled warrior should strike at that rear portion.
Those who are not wounded, not terrified, and not deprived of their armor;
those whose weapons have been dropped and who are fleeing on foot after dismounting from their horses and elephants—these should neither be slain nor oppressed.
Whether he be the sole thread of his lineage or one who has come for refuge, whoever says with palms joined,
"I am yours," you should not slay those who do not fight, nor protectors, nor those protected by women.
Due to portents such as fires in the quarters, dust rising from the earth, showers of stones, thunderbolts, earthquakes, and other such anomalies;
and due to the cries of beasts and birds that are harsh at the conclusion of a battle—even if the king achieves victory, it will not be auspicious for him.
When auspicious beasts and birds appear, when gentle breezes bring delight, when the planets possess clear rays and the circle of the quarters is free from dust,
and when no other portents are seen at the conclusion of the victory— then the king enjoys the enemy’s land in happiness, free from thorns.
Upon reaching the cities and territories of others, the king should not seize the property of virtuous deities, brahmins, or his own kinsmen and women;

he should honor the leading citizens who are devoted to the welfare of the realm, and having entered the city with a joyful army on an auspicious lunar day, karana, and nakshatra, he should dwell there.
That lord of men who, like a leather water-skin, acts according to the instructions of those who know the movements of the celestial spheres,
shall before long attain sovereignty over the entire circle of the earth, just as Purandara does in heaven.
First, the king’s desire to obtain what has not yet been obtained; then, the preservation and increase of what has been obtained;
and finally, the proper distribution of that which has been rightly increased among worthy recipients—this is his true gain.

When benefics are in the angles, and Jupiter, Venus, and the Ascendant are occupied by malefics—provided they are not in the angles or the eighth house—and when the Ascendant is a fixed sign belonging to a domestic animal and is free from the eighth house; one may enter a house when the Moon is auspicious and favorable.
Also, under the asterisms of Revatī, Dhaniṣṭhā, or the Varuṇa group (Śatabhiṣaj), or under the three Uttaras presided over by Svayambhū (Brahmā).
The entry into the house should take place when the moon has not waned, on an auspicious day, and under a lunar date that is not empty.

Having indeed protected the earth according to the Dharma— abounding with reservoirs, groves, and temples— and having provided it with wells and adorned it with funeral mounds, they conquer the worlds of the Lord of the Immortals.
Having approached his own domain,
the lord of men should offer the creepers and the additional gifts according to the prescribed ritual to the hosts of Pramathas, the Asuras, the Bhūtas, and the deities.
The expedition and the descent at the outset, the conduct, and the region to be attacked; the chapter on yoga, the physician, the offering of strength, and likewise the ritual bath.
The causes of fire, the characteristics of the lunar mansions and the moon,
as well as the rules for building halls, the signs of elephants, the administration of musth, and the behavior of horses [should be known].
The ritual for the sword, the departure, augury, the encouragement of troops, and the founding of a city—
this summary of chapters is here briefly indicated.
End of the *Yogayātrā*.
